analysis.one_liner: Lets owners fix their own electronics without breaking copyright law.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on February 2, 2022 and never received a vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Current copyright law makes it illegal to bypass digital locks on electronics, even to fix your own property, and it bars making or selling the tools that would do it. This bill would change that, so anyone could diagnose, maintain, or repair digital equipment without breaking the law. It would carve out medical devices and medical software, leaving their repair rules unchanged.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of phones, tractors, appliances, and other digital equipment, independent repair shops, and electronics recyclers would all gain. If the bill passed, an owner or shop could legally access or bypass the software locks manufacturers use to restrict repair, use or make diagnostic tools and replacement parts, and fix equipment themselves rather than paying the manufacturer for service.

how_it_helps.text: Amends federal copyright law (section 1201 of title 17) so that bypassing a digital access lock is legal when done for the purpose of diagnosing, maintaining, or repairing digital electronic equipment.

Also legalizes making, importing, selling, or providing tools, parts, and services designed to do that circumvention for repair purposes, which means repair shops and parts sellers could operate openly.
Defines 'digital electronic equipment' broadly as any product that depends on attached or embedded digital electronics to function, covering consumer devices and other digitally controlled machines.

Excludes medical devices (as defined in the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act) and medical-setting digital products or embedded software from these repair rights, so manufacturers and distributors in that space keep the copyright restrictions they have today.

analysis.who_pays: Electronics and equipment manufacturers would lose their ability to use copyright law to channel repair work into their own service networks or authorized dealers, and to charge owners for repair access, parts, and diagnostics.

drawbacks.text: Critics of right-to-repair laws warn that opening up repair could let unqualified fixes affect equipment performance, reliability, or safety features.
The bill carves out medical devices entirely, so the equipment doctors and hospitals depend on would stay locked and factory-serviced even though other equipment would be covered.
Manufacturers could lose revenue from proprietary parts and service contracts, which some argue helps fund product development.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For owners of everyday electronics and independent repair shops, the benefit is straightforward: a legal right to fix what you own, with parts and tools available on the open market. The main cost is borne by manufacturers, who lose control and revenue from the repair market. The medical-device carve-out limits the scope of any safety debate, but also means the bill stops short of covering medical equipment.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee when it was introduced and never received a vote or moved further before the two-year congressional session ended.

narrative.text: Representative Mondaire Jones introduced the bill in the House on February 2, 2022.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, which was the only committee action on it.
It never received a floor vote and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill was introduced with the support of Representative Victoria Spartz in addition to Representative Jones.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electronics and equipment manufacturers remain in control of the repair market for their own products, so they are better off. Owners who want to fix their own devices and the independent repair shops serving them still face copyright risk for circumventing repair locks.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Electronics manufacturers, whose repair market control stays intact

for.name: Rep. Mondaire Jones
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to legalize repair-related bypassing of digital locks on electronics.

for.name: Rep. Victoria Spartz
for.what_they_did: Joined as a cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote, so there is no roll call; it had 4 cosponsors, split 1 Republican and 3 Democrats, plus the Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: These companies rely on copyright law and digital locks to restrict repair access and push repair work to their own service networks. The bill would remove that control, costing them revenue and market power but saving owners money.

industries.industry: Independent repair shops and parts sellers
industries.note: The bill would legalize making, selling, and using repair tools and parts for digital electronics, opening the repair market to small independent shops. Their gain runs alongside owners' interests in affordable repair.
The bill explicitly exempts medical devices and medical software, so these manufacturers keep copyright-based restrictions on repair and continue routing service work through their own channels.
